content.title: About
content.content: Ambrosia is a dry concentrate derived from the flowers of annual Ambrosia plants, used in the food industry as a flavoring and mild sweetener. It has a light floral aroma and a subtly sweet taste, commonly employed in confectionery, beverages, and diet products.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “ambrosia” comes from the ancient Greek word meaning “food of the gods.”
The extract is obtained from flowers harvested at the beginning of summer when aromatic compounds are at their peak.
Unlike many synthetic flavorings, ambrosia contains no artificial colorants.
It is frequently used in gluten‑free and vegan recipes because of its neutral flavor profile.
Its polyphenol content makes it a potential natural antioxidant.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in ambrosia help neutralize free radicals and protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A modest amount of dietary fiber aids regular bowel function.

items.title: Low‑calorie flavor enhancer
items.content: Ambrosia adds taste without significantly increasing the caloric content of foods.

items.title: Allergen‑friendly
items.content: Unlike nut‑based flavorings, ambrosia typically does not trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Its phytochemicals may contribute to a stronger immune system.

items.title: Pollen allergy
items.content: People allergic to ambrosia pollen may react to the product.

items.title: Processed additives
items.content: Some commercial versions may contain hidden sweeteners or preservatives.

items.title: Excessive intake
items.content: Large amounts can cause mild gastrointestinal upset due to fiber content.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Phytochemicals might affect the metabolism of certain medications; consult a healthcare professional if you take medicines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add ambrosia to doughs, creams, yogurts, smoothies, and non‑alcoholic drinks. Typically 1–2 g per 100 g of product is enough to impart its characteristic aroma. It can replace sugar in diet recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ambrosia in a sealed container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to preserve its aromatic compounds. Shelf life is usually 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Head cheese is a traditional meat jelly made from boiled meat, natural gelatin, and spices that sets into a firm slice. It is usually prepared from beef, pork, or poultry, often with bones, cartilage and skin to provide gelatin. Served cold, sliced, and commonly accompanied by mustard or vinegar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Head cheese is known worldwide under various names: aspic (France), meat jelly (Germany), galareta (Poland).
It is traditionally made in colder months when ambient temperature helps the jelly set quickly.
In Soviet cuisine, head cheese was a staple for holidays such as New Year and Victory Day.
For a clear jelly, only a clean, fat‑free broth is used.
Some regional recipes add carrots, onions, garlic and spices for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Collagen from bones and cartilage supports skin elasticity, joint health, and connective tissue.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The meat provides a complete set of essential amino acids for tissue repair and growth.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Contains iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Head cheese fits well into low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The broth component helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Insufficiently cooked broth may harbor pathogens; proper heating and handling are essential.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt can make head cheese unsuitable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to certain types of meat.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of gelatin can cause stomach upset in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve head cheese cold, sliced into thin pieces. It is often paired with mustard, vinegar, horseradish or fresh herbs. It can be accompanied by boiled vegetables or potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep head cheese refrigerated, covered with plastic wrap or in an airtight container, for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size pieces, though the texture may change slightly after thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce is a ready‑to‑heat meal that includes cooked pasta, a smooth cream‑based sauce and often additions such as ham, mushrooms or herbs. Packaged in a single‑serve pouch, it only needs to be warmed in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is typically made from heavy cream, butter and grated Parmesan cheese.
Pasta in ready meals is usually cooked al dente to retain texture after reheating.
Fast‑freeze packaging preserves flavor and freshness for up to 12 months.
Some versions use whole‑grain pasta, increasing fiber content.
Cream‑sauce pasta is a popular quick‑lunch option in Europe and North America.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the pasta quickly replenish glycogen stores, providing readily available energy.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cream sauce with Parmesan adds calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Enriched pasta supplies vitamins B1, B2 and B3, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Additions such as ham or chicken boost protein content, aiding tissue repair.

items.title: Fatty acids
items.content: Cream contributes a modest amount of saturated fat and vitamin D.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and added ingredients make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Lactose presence
items.content: Cream and cheese may cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Ready sauces often contain salt; those with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain dairy, gluten and occasionally nut‑derived flavorings.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the pouch in the microwave for 2–3 minutes (or follow package directions), stir, let stand for a minute and serve. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated cheese or a pinch of black pepper if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place at 10 °C–25 °C. After opening, consume within 24 hours and keep refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean pork, boiled rice and vegetables (carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens). It is finished with a soy‑based sauce that adds a savory, slightly sweet flavor and boosts nutritional value with additional protein and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide, especially popular in Asian cuisines.
Rice is the primary source of carbohydrates for more than half of the world’s population.
Broccoli is rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale) contain more vitamin K than any other food.
Soy sauce was invented in China over 2,500 years ago and remains a staple seasoning in many dishes.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork provides complete animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbohydrates that release glucose slowly, helping maintain satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both pork and rice contain thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens are abundant in vitamin C, carotenoids and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Soy sauce adds iron, magnesium and phosphorus, as well as a modest amount of sodium that, in moderate amounts, supports fluid balance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in salt; people with hypertension should limit the amount used.

items.title: Allergies
items.content: Soy sauce contains soy proteins that may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Meat safety
items.content: Improperly handled or undercooked pork may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If vegetables are not washed thoroughly, they may retain pesticide residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing sautéed pork pieces with rice and vegetables. A squeeze of fresh lemon juice or a dash of ginger can brighten the flavor. It works as a standalone meal or as part of a larger menu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C to ensure any bacteria are destroyed.
